At the height of the trade war between Trump and China, with tariffs being raised nearly every week, companies like Logitech responded with sharp price hikes on their products sold in the United States.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled those tariffs illegal and ordered refunds to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing those refunds on to consumers, and a class action lawsuit is now underway in an attempt to address that……

Trump's Tariff Saga

Last year, Trump seized on the U.S. trade deficit with China, seemingly fantasising that slapping massive tariffs on Chinese-made products would force companies like Apple to bring their manufacturing back to America.

This was, of course, never a realistic prospect. The U.S. lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, expertise and affordable labour to support consumer electronics production at the scale required by major brands.

Trump has consistently claimed that China pays the tariffs, but the reality is that the costs are ultimately borne by American brands importing finished goods — and those additional expenses are passed on to consumers in the form of higher prices. At the most chaotic point of this saga, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example: the company raised prices on roughly half of its products by up to 25%.

Consumers Deserve a Refund

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that the money paid by U.S. businesses must be refunded — a process that is now underway.

The problem is that the costs were ultimately borne by consumers through higher prices, yet none of the affected companies have shown any intention of refunding their customers.

The law firm CPM has filed a class action lawsuit against Logitech, seeking to recover refunds for consumers who paid higher prices while the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac's Take

The principle at stake is clear-cut: businesses paid the tariffs, passed the extra cost on to consumers, and now the government is refunding the businesses. Morally speaking, they ought to pass that money back to the consumers who purchased their products during that period.

In practice, however, this is likely to be enormously challenging. Logitech would need to identify every transaction made through the vast network of third-party retailers, track the prices consumers paid, and calculate what portion of those prices was attributable to the tariffs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it could set a very interesting precedent — though it's worth noting that with class actions, it's usually the lawyers who come out ahead, while the average payout to consumers tends to be modest.
